newsitem.title: UK: AIR CRASHES UNLIKELY TO UP INSURANCE RATES - MARKET.
newsitem.headline: AIR CRASHES UNLIKELY TO UP INSURANCE RATES - MARKET.

text.p: A spate of aircraft accidents in the last week has not yet exceeded the norm for the year and is unlikely to lead to a sudden upturn in insurance rates, market experts said.
"I've been speaking to people this morning and they're not convinced it's enough to have an impact on rates," one London-based aviation underwriter told Reuters on Wednesday.
Aviation insurance rates have been falling steadily since 1993, with many in the market reporting decreases of around 20 percent this year.
However, with the autumn renewal season coming up for most world airlines, recent events would focus minds, Richard Maylam, chairman of the Lloyd's Aviation Underwriters Association, said.
"This will certainly make underwriters nervous and could help stabilise rates, but it's really too early to say," he added.
The total of insured hull losses in the past week is now approaching $200 million following yesterday's crash of a Korean Air Lines Boeing 747 on Guam with heavy loss of life.
The KAL aircraft was insured for around $60 million. However, the biggest loss of the past week was a Federal Express cargo aircraft insured for $115 million.
Three other passenger aircraft have also been damaged or destroyed in the last week, but none is expected to lead to a large insurance claim.
An ATR-42 which crashed at Florence airport has been declared a total constructive loss and was insured for $14.5 million.
A British Aerospace ATP airliner was damaged when it landed on two wheels at Manchester airport on Sunday, while on Monday an Air Afrique Boeing 737 was damaged by fire at Douala airport, Cameroon.
The 1969 built Air Afrique Boeing was worth around $3.0 million, aviation sources said.

Another London based aviation insurer said that the recent clutch of accidents was out of the ordinary in such a short period, but had to be seen in the context of a very light year so far for air accidents.

The cost of hull losses for western built jets in the first six months was $168.6 million, compared with almost $200 million in the same period last year, consultancy Airclaims said in a recent report.
The FedEx hull claim is the third largest in aviation history and would remind people of the scale of aviation risks, one broker said.
However, others in the market noted that the aviation insurance market is still awash with capacity and this will act as a brake on any upward pressure on rates.
Insurers said it was too early to calculate passenger liability claims from the KAL crash.
